newsitem.title: UK: Dlr softer in late Europe but new upmove awaited.
newsitem.headline: Dlr softer in late Europe but new upmove awaited.

text.p: The dollar drifted gently lower in the European session, but traders saw it gathering strength for the next upmove as it consolidated the week's chunky gains.

Comments from a German finance ministry official giving the hard line on meeting EMU criteria knocked dollar/mark, but market watchers said the growing conviction that Germany was unfazed by its currency's weakness limited the damage.

Dollar/yen also bowed out of European dealings slightly softer than on Wednesday. Data released overnight showing Japan's contentious trade surplus rose less than expected in June kept the U.S. unit underpinned, however.
The dollar was quoted at 1.7915/20 marks and 116.01/06 yen at 1546 GMT, down from late Wednesday's European levels of 1.7976/81 and 116.40/50 respectively.
But traders and analysts were sanguine, especially after the U.S. July Philadelphia survey far exceeded expectations with a reading of 28.1 compared to the forecast 18.0 and June's 25.2.
"It's an early signal things are still motoring along in manufacturing," said Ken Wattret, senior economist at Banque Paribas in London.
Friday's release of June's key German Ifo business indices will be closely watched by the market, though.
Speculation has been rife that the Ifo research institute's report will show business activity strengthening.
"For mark weakness to turn around you need to see a change in perception of the German economy and a strong Ifo could help," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago here.
The market buzzed with vague talk throughout the day of European central bank intervention to support the mark. Milan traders reported that the Bank of Italy had sold lire for marks.
But dealers saw precious little to support rumours of other intervention, and said the fear of concerted central bank action -- which has blocked the dollar's upward path -- was receding.
German government officials have, in any case, played down the mark's woes recently and traders said that has helped allay fears of intervention.
"The Germans don't mind a weak mark -- it's the only thing that's going to drag their economy back up," said a dealer at a U.S. bank in London.

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer gave dollar/mark just brief pause for thought in late Europe when he said he hoped the mark's correction against the dollar would "not come to an overreaction". He also said he was watching foreign exchange market developments "very carefully".

Earlier, the dollar stumbled and the mark climbed on its European crosses after senior German Finance Ministry official Hansgeorg Hauser said Germany would insist on a strict interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty when it came to choosing which countries would qualify for European monetary union.
The conviction that monetary union will begin with a broad swathe of members, breeding a euro which is weaker than the mark, has been a major factor in the German unit's decline.
Dollar/yen was supported overnight after data showed Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus rose more than 934 billion yen on the year, below the forecast increase of over a trillion yen.

Nevertheless, the contrast with the U.S. trade situation remains glaring, analysts said. Figures out on Friday are expected to show the U.S. May trade deficit widening to $9.2 billion from April's $8.4 billion.

As well as that and the Ifo report, a major market focus tomorrow will be a meeting of the EU monetary committee. Traders said the committee might address the issue of confidence in the euro, and encourage a brake on dollar/mark.
The mark ended higher on its crosses, at 972.25/45 lire versus late Wednesday's level here of 970.60/90.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
